summary: An index-style memo that summarizes the RFCs numbered 3000 through 3099, listing what each one is. It is an informational reference for finding documents in that range.

eli5.summary: It is like a table of contents for a shelf of one hundred books, telling you what each book is about.

subtitle: An index and guide to RFCs published from 3000 through 3099

tldr.problem: Over 100 RFCs were published in the 3000-3099 range between January and November 2001, covering diverse topics. It is difficult to understand what each one is about without reading all of them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3099 provides a single-page entry for each RFC in the 3000-3099 range, listing the author, publication date, title, and a brief one-paragraph summary of what the RFC specifies or discusses.
tldr.outcome: Readers can quickly browse the full range and identify which RFCs are relevant to their needs, or see which standards track RFCs in that range are relevant to their work.

facts.label: Entries provided
facts.value: One per RFC with author, date, title, and summary

today: RFC 3099 was published in November 2001 as a reference document summarizing RFCs in the 3000-3099 range. As an informational summary, it has not been obsoleted. However, the document's status field and implementation information are accurate only as of November 2001; readers needing current standards track status should consult the latest Internet Official Protocol Standards document. Similar summary RFCs have been published for other ranges (RFC 4000-4099, RFC 5000-5099, etc.), providing historical documentation of Internet standardization work in each era.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 3099 is a summary and index of 100 RFCs (RFC 3000 through RFC 3099) published between January and November 2001. This is a reference document that helps readers navigate a significant range of the RFC series.

The RFC provides one entry per RFC, showing the RFC number, author, publication date, title, and a brief description of what that RFC covers. Some entries note that an RFC is on the standards track, meaning it is part of the formal Internet standardization process.

This document is similar in purpose to RFC 2000 (RFC 2000-2099 summary), RFC 1000 (RFC 1000-1099 summary), and other such summary RFCs published periodically to help readers find documents in a given numerical range.
sections.eli5: Instead of reading all hundred books on the shelf, this document gives you one sentence about each one so you can decide which ones to open.

sections.title: Coverage and Organization
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs in the 3000-3099 range cover a wide variety of Internet technologies and protocols, published over the course of a year. The RFCs include:

  • Standards track RFCs: protocols being formalized through the IETF standardization process, such as routing protocols, cryptographic authentication schemes, header compression techniques, and protocol extensions.
  • Informational RFCs: guidance, best practices, vendor specifications, and documentation that provide useful information without specifying standards. This category includes RFC 3098 (responsible email advertising) and RFC 3094 (TALI signaling gateway interface).
  • Experimental RFCs: protocols and mechanisms proposed for evaluation and discussion before standardization.

Each entry lists the RFC number, the author or organization, the month and year of publication, the full title, and a summary paragraph. The RFC notes that some RFCs may change status during standards processing, so readers are directed to the current "Internet Official Protocol Standards" document for definitive status.
sections.eli5: The hundred RFCs include both official standards and unofficial guidance documents from different parts of the Internet community.

sections.title: Examples from the Range
sections.content:
The 3000-3099 range includes a diverse collection. Some noteworthy examples illustrate the breadth:

  • RFC 3095 (ROHC): a standards track RFC specifying robust header compression for RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP, and ESP/IP headers used in mobile networks.
  • RFC 3098: informational guidance on responsible email and newsgroup advertising practices.
  • RFC 3094: informational specification of Tekelec's Transport Adapter Layer Interface for carrying SS7 signaling over IP.
  • RFC 3092: an April 1st (joke) RFC exploring the etymology of the metasyntactic variable "foo."
  • RFC 3070: a standards track RFC describing how to deploy Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) over Frame Relay circuits.

This sampling shows how a single 100-RFC range can contain fundamental protocols, vendor specifications, practical guidance, and even humor.
sections.eli5: Among the hundred RFCs you will find serious protocols, good advice on marketing, translator specifications, jokes, and everything in between.

sections.title: Standards Track Status
sections.content:
The RFC notes that many (but not all) RFCs in the 3000-3099 range are on the standards track, meaning they have been accepted by the IETF as formal standardization work. These RFCs are being processed as Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Full Standards.

However, the status of an RFC can change over time. An RFC might start as a Proposed Standard, become a Draft Standard, be reclassified as Historic, or be obsoleted by a newer RFC. The summary entries in RFC 3099 reflect status at the time of publication; readers seeking current status should consult the official "Internet Official Protocol Standards" (STD 1) document for the most up-to-date information.

The distinction is important: a standards track RFC has undergone IETF review and has a defined path toward (or history of) standardization, while an informational RFC provides useful information without going through the same rigorous process.
sections.eli5: Some RFCs are official Internet standards being developed; others are just helpful documents. The real status of any RFC can change, so you should check the official list if status matters for your project.
